document_purpose: evidence-based clinical practice guidelines for the management of Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (T1DM) in India, published by the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR)
specialist_role: endocrinologist or diabetologist specializing in Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus management
analyst_role: clinical guideline analyst or medical content specialist reviewing diabetes care recommendations
entity_types: diabetes type (Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus, T2DM, FCPD, mitochondrial diabetes)
treatment regimen (insulin therapy, dietary management, exercise protocols)
diagnostic criteria (staging, classification, differentiation from other diabetes types)
monitoring parameters (blood glucose, ketone levels, HbA1c)

key_terminology.T2DM: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus, characterized by insulin resistance and relative insulin deficiency
key_terminology.FCPD: Fibrocalculous Pancreatic Diabetes, a form of diabetes associated with pancreatic calcification
key_terminology.DKA: Diabetic Ketoacidosis, a life-threatening complication of diabetes characterized by hyperglycemia, ketosis, and acidosis
key_terminology.RDA: Recommended Dietary Allowance, the average daily intake level sufficient to meet nutrient requirements
key_terminology.HbA1c: Glycated hemoglobin, a measure of average blood glucose levels over 2-3 months
key_terminology.BG: Blood Glucose, the concentration of glucose in the blood

labeling_few_shots.text_snippet: Vitamin and mineral requirements in children with diabetes are the same as in other healthy children. There is no clear evidence to suggest that routine vitamin or mineral supplementation in children with diabetes is beneficial.
labeling_few_shots.description: Guidance on vitamin and mineral supplementation for pediatric diabetes patients, emphasizing adherence to standard dietary recommendations without routine supplementation.

labeling_few_shots.text_snippet: Apart from bacterial infections, rare fungal infections like rhinocerebral mucormycosis and pulmonary aspergillosis are seen at an increased incidence in patients with DKA.
labeling_few_shots.description: Identification of rare but serious fungal infections associated with diabetic ketoacidosis, highlighting the need for heightened clinical suspicion.

labeling_few_shots.text_snippet: Glucosuria due to uncontrolled hyperglycemia is associated with increased risk of urinary tract infections.
labeling_few_shots.description: Link between glucosuria from uncontrolled hyperglycemia and elevated risk of urinary tract infections, emphasizing the importance of glycemic control.

delta_few_shots.topic: carbohydrate counting in insulin dose adjustment
delta_few_shots.version_a: Carbohydrate counting was recommended for patients using multiple daily insulin injections to estimate mealtime insulin doses.
delta_few_shots.version_b: Carbohydrate counting is now recommended for all insulin-treated patients, including those on insulin pumps, with standardized training programs introduced for healthcare providers.
delta_few_shots.analysis: The earlier version focused on carbohydrate counting primarily for MDI users. The updated guideline expands this practice to all insulin-dependent patients and mandates standardized provider training, reflecting broader adoption of carbohydrate counting in diabetes technology and a shift toward more precise insulin dosing across all treatment modalities.

delta_few_shots.topic: target blood glucose ranges in pediatric T1DM
delta_few_shots.version_a: Target blood glucose ranges for children with T1DM were set at 80–180 mg/dL before meals and 100–180 mg/dL at bedtime.
delta_few_shots.version_b: Target blood glucose ranges for children with T1DM are now set at 90–150 mg/dL before meals and 100–180 mg/dL at bedtime to reduce hypoglycemia risk.
delta_few_shots.analysis: The updated guideline reverses the previous recommendation by tightening pre-meal targets to reduce hypoglycemia risk in pediatric patients, reflecting new evidence on the benefits of lower glycemic variability in this vulnerable population.

qna_few_shots.q: Why did the guideline change the recommended blood glucose targets for children with T1DM?
qna_few_shots.a: The change was driven by emerging evidence showing that tighter pre-meal glucose targets (90–150 mg/dL) reduce hypoglycemia risk without increasing overall hyperglycemia burden in pediatric patients. The previous range (80–180 mg/dL) was associated with higher rates of hypoglycemic events, particularly overnight.

qna_few_shots.q: How should healthcare providers implement the new carbohydrate counting recommendations for insulin pump users?
qna_few_shots.a: Providers should ensure all insulin pump users receive standardized carbohydrate counting training, including use of integrated bolus calculators and real-time glucose monitoring data. The guideline now requires documentation of carbohydrate counting accuracy in pump settings to optimize mealtime insulin dosing.

evolution_few_shot.topic: carbohydrate counting in insulin dose adjustment
evolution_few_shot.foundation: Carbohydrate counting was initially recommended only for patients using multiple daily insulin injections to estimate mealtime insulin doses.
value_added: Expanded to all insulin-treated patients, including those on insulin pumps
Mandated standardized training programs for healthcare providers
Integrated with real-time glucose monitoring data for dynamic insulin dosing
evolution_few_shot.narrative: The original guideline established carbohydrate counting as a key tool for patients on MDI regimens. The updated version builds on this foundation by broadening its application to all insulin-dependent patients and embedding it within modern diabetes technologies. This evolution enables more precise and individualized insulin dosing, improving glycemic outcomes across diverse treatment modalities.
